title: Complex numbers, from j to AC circuits
hook: Say a coil draws 23 A from a 230 V supply. Why does wiring a capacitor across it, a second path drawing 23 A of its own, cut the supply current to about 21 A?
oneBreath: Multiplying by −1 turns an arrow half way round, so call the quarter turn j: done twice it gives −1, and numbers become arrows on a flat plane, each with an across part and an up part. Arrows add tip to tail and multiply by stretching and turning, so each can be written as across-and-up or as a length and an angle, whichever suits the sum. A coil or a capacitor opposes AC by a size at a quarter turn, so one such number holds a circuit's whole opposition, and Ohm's law, series and parallel work just as they do for DC.

ideas.title: A number whose square is minus one
ideas.oneLine: Times −1 is a half turn, so j, the quarter turn that done twice makes it, is a number with j × j = −1.

ideas.title: The complex plane, and adding
ideas.oneLine: Add complex numbers real with real and j with j, which lays their arrows tip to tail on a plane: real across, j up.

ideas.title: Multiplying: stretch and turn
ideas.oneLine: Multiply complex numbers like two brackets, putting j × j = −1, and see the answer is the first arrow stretched and turned.

ideas.title: The conjugate, and dividing
ideas.oneLine: Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the bottom's conjugate, its mirror image with the j part's sign flipped, which makes the bottom real.

ideas.title: Polar form: length and angle
ideas.oneLine: Convert a + jb to length and angle, r∠θ, with Pythagoras and tan⁻¹, checking the quarter on a sketch, and back with cos and sin.

ideas.title: Multiplying and dividing in polar form
ideas.oneLine: In length-and-angle form, multiply by multiplying the lengths and adding the angles, and divide by dividing the lengths and taking the angles away.

ideas.title: Impedance: Z = R + jX
ideas.oneLine: Impedance R + jX is resistance plus reactance, the opposition to AC of a coil (+j) or a capacitor (−j), all in ohms.

ideas.title: Ohm's law with j: series and parallel
ideas.oneLine: V = IZ with complex impedances, combined in series and parallel by your DC rules, gives each current's size and its angle from the voltage.

calibration.q: Which number, multiplied by itself, gives −9?
options: None of the ordinary positive or negative numbers
calibration.why: 3 × 3 = 9, and −3 × −3 = 9 too, because minus times minus is plus, so no ordinary number squares to a negative. −3 is the common slip: it forgets that the second minus cancels the first.

calibration.q: You walk 30 m along a wall, turn a right angle and walk 40 m. How far are you, in a straight line, from where you started?
calibration.why: The two walks are arrows at a right angle, so Pythagoras gives √(30² + 40²) = 50 m. 70 m adds the lengths as if both walks went the same way; 10 m takes one from the other, as if they went opposite ways.
